newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Docklands bombing ended hopes of Northern Irish peace.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Docklands bombing ended hopes of Northern Irish peace.

text.p: Northern Ireland's dream of peace ended abruptly one year ago on February 9 when IRA guerrillas bombed a London complex. Twelve months later, the dream is a continuing and worsening nightmare.

Police, security experts and politicians believe that the Irish Republican Army bomb which killed two people at London's Canary Wharf heralded the start of a new campaign to make Northern Ireland ungovernable for any British government.
"Their aim is to drive the British out of Northern Ireland," said security specialist Jim Cusack of the IRA's Canary Wharf bomb, which ended a 17-month truce and the peace dreams with it.
"They tried in the past but have never succeeded. The only way to do it, in their view, is to make the place ungovernable," Cusack, security editor of Dublin's Irish Times told Reuters.

As British political parties square up for a spring election, the IRA, Europe's oldest underground fighting force, is sending them bellicose signals that its attacks are bound to intensify as the poll nears, security analysts forecast.
The IRA, in the 28th year of a war to end British rule, says Britain must give its Sinn Fein political wing a seat at talks on the province's future before it calls a ceasefire.

Britain is adamant it will not permit the IRA to bomb its way to the talks and that any new truce must mark a complete end to violence, not a tactical truce to see how far Sinn Fein might get at the negotiating table.
IRA'S ARMY COUNCIL SAID TO ORDER MORE HITS

"From what I understand, all (IRA) brigades in Northern Ireland have had orders from their army council' to carry out attacks on good quality security targets,' said Paul Connolly, security correspondent of the Belfast Telegraph.

British security sources say current IRA violence, which has yet to claim its first 1997 fatality, is aimed at provoking its pro-British Loyalist foes into ending their own two-year truce and going back on the warpath.
The IRA apparently aims to render Northern Ireland so turbulent that the next British government will make it a top agenda item and get Sinn Fein to peace talks at any price.

"They (the IRA) seem to believe that there is no chance of movement this side of a general election and they believe that the only way they are going to squeeze any concessions or movement out of the British government is by a resumption of a certain level of violence," Connolly said.

"It could be to send a message to the incoming governent that we haven't gone away'." The IRA abandoned its truce accusing Britain of reneging on what it said was a promise that an IRA truce would earn Sinn Fein a seat at the talks. Britain insisted that the guerrillas pledge to start disarming to show good faith - the IRA refused.
Two Londoners were killed on February 9 by a massive IRA lorry-bomb that ripped through the British capital's prestigious Docklands financial zone causing millions of pounds of damage.
In the rubble too, lay a carefully crafted Anglo-Irish led peace process that had depended on a permanent end to IRA violence and all-party talks as twin cornerstones.
But the IRA's English bombing campaign designed "to strike at the heart of the enemy" was jolted in its tracks by British intelligence successes that scooped explosives and suspects.
BRITISH INTELLIGENCE STRIKES BACK AT IRA

"They made inroads into two or three terrorist cells but...there are one and possibly two still active on the mainland," said Connolly. "The IRA intention would still be to inflict maximum damage in Britain."
Forced back into its familiar ambush territory of sprawling Northern Irish housing estates and country lanes, the IRA is conducting a war that risks a violent Loyalist backlash.
Few are optimistic about a breakthrough before a general election which Britain's Prime Minister John Major must call by late May.
Politicians say the guerrillas have returned to a "bomb and ballot box" strategy to give Britain a foretaste of what could happen if Sinn Fein is kept out of talks.

Brendan O'Leary, professor of political science at the London School of Economics, doubts that the IRA will call a pre-election ceasefire, which Protestant Unionists say is possible in a vote-catching bid for Sinn Fein.
"I think it is more likely that they would call one in the aftermath of an election," he told Reuters.
IRA TRUCE SEEN AFTER UK ELECTION

"I think that they went back to to war as a result of internal tensions within their own organisation...The hardliners' position was that the ceasefire was being taken advantage of by a British government which was not delivering on its promise of all-party-negotations."

When the IRA called its first lengthy ceasefire in September 1994, Britain demanded proof that its "cessation" was genuine and still insists that a credible guerrilla truce is the only ticket that Sinn Fein needs for a talks place.
Cusack says IRA hawks have rebuffed the peace strategies of Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams, who has shaped the party's "peace strategy" since the mid 1980s.
"The (Docklands) explosives were in place for probably more than a year. By December 1995 Adams had lost the argument within the Republican movement (comprising Sinn Fein and IRA).
"The hardliners are as hardline as ever. They are as far away from ceasefire talk or thinking as they have been in the past 25 years," Cusack said.
O'Leary says a bi-partisan policy between Britain's ruling Conservatives and the opposition Labour leader, and putative prime minister Tony Blair, has stifled Northern Ireland as a political issue.

"I think an important question from the viewpoint of an incoming British government will be whether or not it believes that it can get a renewal of the IRA ceasefire on the original conditions. If it could, I suspect it would be willing to deliver rapid entry (for Sinn Fein) into negotiations, he said.
